slides.notes: Each student ranks three of five reasons; the result uses a Borda count. Use the top reason as the thread of the lecture: every section that follows returns to it. Section 1 answers why regions matter, section 2 how to measure them from space, and section 3 which tools to use.

Large development gaps within countries (Rio de Janeiro)

slide.title: Drop a pin on the poorest part of this photo

slides.notes: The Rio de Janeiro photo, now as a pin board. Most pins should land on the informal settlement in the foreground, a few on the high-rise blocks. Ask the room what visual cues they used: roofs, density, roads, green space. Those cues are exactly what daytime satellite images measure in section 2.
slides.title: Drop a pin on the poorest part of this photo

slide.title: How would you measure the development gap in this photo? Name one indicator

slides.notes: The slide asked how we can measure, predict and explain these gaps. Collect indicators for 90 seconds, then open voting (two votes each) and read the top three. Point out which ones need a survey and which ones can be seen from above.
slides.title: How would you measure the development gap in this photo? Name one indicator
Gaps show clear geospatial patterns (Sao Paulo)

slide.heading: This Sao Paulo photo was taken in 2004. By 2021, the gap between the two neighborhoods was...

slides.notes: A prediction poll; do not reveal the answer. The next slide shows the same spot in 2004 and 2021: the favela of Paraisopolis and the luxury towers next to it look almost unchanged, and El Pais (2022) reported that little has changed in nearly 20 years. The answer is B, about the same: gaps can persist for decades.

Local development matters for several SDGs

slide.title: Tap each goal: why does it need local data?

config.title: Tap each goal: why does it need local data?

hotspots.title: SDG 11: Cities and communities
hotspots.description: Slums, transport and housing differ block by block, so a national average hides the neighborhoods in need.

hotspots.title: Leave no one behind
hotspots.description: The 2030 Agenda asks for data disaggregated by location, not only by country.

hotspots.title: SDG 10: Reduced inequalities
hotspots.description: Inequality between regions is part of total inequality and only shows up in subnational data.

hotspots.title: SDG 13: Climate action
hotspots.description: Floods, droughts and heat hit specific places, so adaptation needs local exposure maps.

hotspots.title: SDG 8: Decent work and growth
hotspots.description: Growth is uneven across regions; local data show where jobs and income are rising or falling.

slides.notes: Students tap the numbered pins on their phones and read at their own pace while you talk through the slide. No scoring. Ask which goal matters most in their own country, which leads into the next ranking.
slides.title: Tap each goal: why does it need local data?

slide.title: Which goal most needs data for small regions? Rank your top three

slides.notes: No right answer. Many students put SDG 1 first: poverty maps are the classic use of subnational data. Note the goal that ranks last and ask one student to argue for it.
slides.title: Which goal most needs data for small regions? Rank your top three
But... do we have enough data?

slide.heading: Do we have enough data to study regional development in your country?
options: Only for large regions such as states
No, data are scarce or outdated

slides.notes: An honest answer from the room before the data tour. Students from countries with recent censuses tend to answer A or B. Keep the result in mind: section 2 argues that satellites fill exactly the gap behind answers B and C.
slides.title: Do we have enough data to study regional development in your country?

slide.heading: Next video: Rosling starts in 1810. In that year, life expectancy in every country was below...

slides.notes: Answer: A, 40 years. In 1810 all countries were poor and sick, with life expectancy below 40. The four-minute video that follows shows 200 years of divergence and then convergence. Play it in full (core).
slides.title: Next video: Rosling starts in 1810. In that year, life expectancy in every country was below...
200 Countries, 200 Years, 4 Minutes (Hans Rosling, BBC)
slides.notes: Play in full, about 4 minutes.

slide.heading: Now Rosling splits China into provinces. Rich Shanghai matches which country in health and wealth?

slides.notes: Answer: B, Italy. The next video starts at 3:40, where Rosling splits China: Shanghai has the health and wealth of Italy, the inland province Guizhou is like Pakistan, and the poorest rural west is like Ghana. One country holds the whole world inside it.
slides.title: Now Rosling splits China into provinces. Rich Shanghai matches which country in health and wealth?
200 Countries, 200 Years: China provinces segment (Hans Rosling, BBC)
slides.notes: Starts at 3:40; stop after the China provinces, about 1 minute.

slide.heading: Match each part of China to the country it resembles (Rosling, 2009)

slides.notes: Answer: Shanghai is Italy, Guizhou is Pakistan, the rural west is Ghana. The point for the course: a national average for China describes none of these places. That is the case for subnational data.
slides.title: Match each part of China to the country it resembles (Rosling, 2009)
slides.answer: Shanghai = Italy; Guizhou province = Pakistan; The poorest rural west = Ghana

slide.heading: The McKinsey study Pixels of Progress splits the world into how many micro regions?

slides.notes: Answer: C. Pixels of Progress (McKinsey Global Institute) uses more than 40,000 micro regions, about 230 times more granular than a country view; each averages about 180,000 people. Night lights helped build it. The next two slides show one bubble for the world and then the world through a regional microscope.
slides.title: The McKinsey study Pixels of Progress splits the world into how many micro regions?
The disaggregation of development (one bubble)

slide.title: A world average of 73 years of life and USD 16,800 of income per person describes most places well.

config.question: A world average of 73 years of life and USD 16,800 of income per person describes most places well.

slides.notes: Answer: False. The single bubble on the previous slide hides a wide cloud of micro regions, far above and below the average in both life expectancy and income, as the next slide shows. Averages are a summary, not a description.

Micro regions as pixels: a raster is an array of values

slide.title: Complete the definition of a raster image

config.question: A raster image is a grid of [blank], and each one stores a [blank].

slides.notes: Answer: pixels, value. A raster is a set of pixels and also an array of numbers, which is why satellite images can enter a regression like any other data. Polygons and points are vector data, the other main type of spatial data.
slides.title: Complete the definition of a raster image

An Introduction to Geospatial Data and GeoQuery (AidData)
slides.notes: Play the first 2 minutes.

slide.title: GeoQuery requires coding or mapping software.

config.question: GeoQuery requires coding or mapping software.

slides.notes: Answer: False. GeoQuery (AidData) filters and aggregates geospatial data to provinces or districts and returns a spreadsheet, without code or mapping software. That makes it the easiest entry point for the portal stop that follows the tour.

slide.heading: Portal stop: find one subnational indicator for your country. Write the indicator, the portal and the level (state, district or pixel).

slides.notes: The hands-on stop, about eight minutes on laptops. Portals: http://geo.aiddata.org, https://globaldatalab.org, https://sedac.ciesin.columbia.edu, https://pipmaps.worldbank.org/en/data/datatopics/poverty-portal/home, https://developers.google.com/earth-engine/datasets, https://gee-community-catalog.org. Suggest GeoQuery or Global Data Lab for beginners. Walk around and help. Close by reading three answers that use different levels, and ask which level would be best for their own research question.
slides.title: Portal stop: find one subnational indicator for your country. Write the indicator, the portal and the level (state, district or pixel).

slide.heading: Match each portal to what it offers

pairs.right_item: Data aggregated to provinces and districts, no code

slides.notes: Answer as listed. Earth Engine and the community catalog are the raster archives behind many of these products; they return in Part 3 with Earth Engine itself.
slides.title: Match each portal to what it offers
slides.answer: AidData GeoQuery = Data aggregated to provinces and districts, no code; Global Data Lab = A subnational Human Development Index; NASA SEDAC = Population and socioeconomic grids; World Bank poverty portal = Subnational poverty maps from surveys
